First he would determine the gender of an individual, and if this could not be determined by an examination of the external genitalia it would be done by examining the pelvic bone, the skull, and the long bones, and in that order. Secondly, he would establish the age range of each individual by examining changes in certain bones by relying on Bosnian population-specific standards. The relevant age ranges were 8 to 12, 13 to 24, and over 25 years of age. Then he would calculate the minimum number of individuals at the site in question and this was done by adding together the total of the most commonly occurring bone in each age range. Only a unique bone or one of a pair of bones would be used for this calculation; for example, if there were 38 left proximal femurs in the 13 to 24 age range, and 48 right proximal tibia in the 25 and over age range, that would give a minimum number of 86 individuals for that total site. To avoid overcounting, the human remains from a primary and any known secondary sites were examined together using the same bone as a basis of the calculations. Mr. Baraybar concluded that between 1996 and 1999, a minimum number of 1.883 individuals had been exhumed by the ICTY from Srebrenica-related graves. Mr. Baraybar also testified that in 1999 he supervised the exhumation of mass graves at Nova Kasaba, at Konjevic Polje, and the site known as Glogova 2. And this continues -- this completes my summary of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And this report -- in this report, you use a new terminology. You use a term that's called the minimum minimal number of individuals exhumed by the ICTY forensic team. Can you briefly explain to us the difference between the minimum number of individuals and the minimum minimal number of individuals?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Sure. Let me start from the beginning. Whenever you -- whenever you exhume a grave with people inside, the logical way to account for the number of bodies in a grave would be a head count typically. But what would happen if you do not have complete bodies but bits and pieces of people? Then things would be slightly more complicated. You may be counting the heads but perhaps the legs will be more common than the heads. So you have to find another way. The other way is called the minimal number of individuals, also known as MNI. And this means from whatever has been found, how many people at least represented. So let's take an example. Imagine that a human skeleton contains 206 bones and if you have a body that is decayed and is cut into pieces, so you will have plenty of possibilities to count elements. So what you have to do is to choose one of a pair, if you got two legs, you will choose the right or the left, or single bones are not duplicated, for example, the first cervical vertebra, there is only one in each individual and you will count it. Based on that, you will basically count the most popular bone of that kind. As a matter of fact, you will count all the bones, I will define which one is the most common, and that will be your minimal number of individuals for that site. But just let's add another layer of confusion that actually happens in reality. We have been assuming that I can count the most popular bone or element in that assemblage, but that is that we are assuming that all individuals are of the same age, so if I have 25 adults, I may count 25 right legs and I will know that at least I have 25 people. But what happened if to those 25 I have to add children of different ages that may not be represented by those right legs? What about if the children between 0 and 3 years are represented by a left arm, and those coming after that are represented by a left leg? So I cannot simply use in that case the right leg because I will be misrepresenting or excluding people that exist, that I can see, so I will need to combine. So this minimal number of individuals will become slightly more complicated because I will need to count the right legs of the adults, the left leg of the children, and whatever arms of the other children as well, and the addition of those three criteria will give me still a number. That will be the minimal number of individuals found in that grave, in that specific grave. Now, what actually happened when we calculated this minimal minimum number, that is pretty much a play with words because there isn't a term for that, would be how to merge into a single number all the bodies that the Tribunal was excavating from 1996 to 2001. The minimal number of individuals per site was not necessarily the same for all the cases. In one site I would have legs, in another one I would have arms, so I cannot simply just add the numbers obtained for each of the sites because I will have an overrepresentation of bodies. So in order to be very conservative it is better to do an underestimate rather than an overestimate. So we have to find the common body part to all sites and to use the same one per age and add it together. And based on that we got a figure of 2.541 individuals represented by all those sites, that is at least 2.541, at least. So it is a very low number because if I add them -- add all the minimal number of individuals I would have over 3.000 people, but that would not be correct because I would know I would be swelling up the numbers. So we have erred on the side of being conservative rather than overestimating. Would that be clear, Ms. Lee?

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: May I please tender this document 65 ter number 05346 into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar, the number will be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2091, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2091 is admitted into evidence. Could I ask one question in relation to this. You divided the bodies you found in age groups. Let's just assume that in one age group the left leg is the most common one which you used. Whereas for the next age group it would be the right. Now, how precise is your determination of the age group? Is it possible, well, let's say that for someone of 25 years, whether that will be 24 and a half or 25 and a half, that you nevertheless would have a double representation once the leg defined as belonging to the category 25 and over and their right leg and the other leg, the left leg, estimated as to belong to the group of up to 25 years, and that left leg being counted as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Extremely good point and the answer is yes. Remember that age estimation is most accurate when you have a complete body because you're not looking at one single, I mean, segment of the body. For example, if I had a complete body, I would be combining different indicators that are found in different parts of the body, but if I have a leg I'm very limited to how much I can say about that leg. I can say, well, it is an adult that is why the plus 25 category. I do not know if this person is 27, 28 and a half, or 45. It is impossible to say. Obviously by looking at it we could go into other type of techniques that could be used but that have a number of problems as well, but that is not the case at the moment. So it is definitely true that there can be an overlap between age categories and that is a total fact and that is why our calculations are so conservative, but so conservative taking into account that we have that possibility of, I mean, double counting, so in order not to double count we rather say we will exclude -- for example, we have two sites. In one site - I don't know - the left leg is more popular and the other one -- is that the right leg is more popular, we would use still the left leg of the other site; that is, undercounting a number of people in order not to overcount because the problem you pointed out is a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you say that's limited to one site where this can happen but is then eliminated --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- by using this same common feature for all sites together.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But did I understand you well that you would still work on the basis of age groups.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So for all the sites possibly for 25 and older, using the left leg and for up to 25 using the right leg, which would then still have not eliminated perfectly the possible overlap between the age groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes and no. Let me just be precise here. Age estimation of younger people, meaning below age 25, is much more precise than age determination on the group 25 and plus because since young people is -- I mean are growing, you have a number of elements that you can still distinguish. So it is less likely that we have overlap or overcounting on younger people than on older people. Older people would be a much more generic group in which case the correction comes from excluding the most popular -- I mean elements per site. I do not believe we have much overlap on the younger ages because they can be separated much more clearly, you know. In the older ones there could be, but I mean we are excluding by using the same common denominator to all the sites.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But there still is a small risk that you have qualified one left bone as under 25 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- perhaps 24 and a half, and the -- another leg be qualified as 25 and older.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Totally. I mean, we admit -- we admit -- I mean, this is not a perfect -- that was not the perfect conditions, I mean, to work because of the level of fragmentation of the remains, and age estimation certainly is better done when you have multiple indicators than you have one single indicator, and finally we got also biological variation meaning that within a normal range or known range we got somebody maturing earlier, maturing later. There could be one individual within a population so it is true, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: May I please have 65 ter number 11016, and this is a preliminary report on the anthropology examination of human remains from the graves at Kevljani in Western Bosnia, and it is dated 8 December 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And Mr. Baraybar, do you recognise this document as one that you drafted?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And may I also please have 65 ter number 11017.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And this is a summary of findings at the secondary mass grave-site of Jakarina Kosa in Western Bosnia, and it is dated the 12th of June, 2002. Mr. Baraybar, do you recognise this document as one that you drafted?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender these both documents 11016 and 11017 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that there are no objections. Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 11016.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Will be Exhibit P2092, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted. 65 ter 11017.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Will be Exhibit P2093.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2093 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, we have looked at several reports today. Do you stand by the analysis and conclusion of all of these reports today?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And was the same methodology used in calculating the minimal number of individuals, minimum minimal number of individuals, and in determining the sex and age of the bones in all of these reports?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And from your examination of human remains, bodies in Bosnia, were you able to determine the time of death of the victims? Just looking at the bones.

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No. The time of death -- or rather than the time, the date of death was not determined on a cursory look at the remains.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And what were they determined -- what were the factors that would determine them?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: We have an indirect way of dating death based on indicators found in the graves or on the bodies such as ID cards with names on it, they were in turn checked with the International Committee of the Red Cross book on the missing that determined that that person would have been last seen at a specific date. In addition to that, the way all the documents such as ICRC letters, and in one case, as far as I remember, an ID card from the Dutch Battalion with a laundry -- identification of somebody as working in the laundry of the Dutch Battalion. So there were a number of elements associated to the remains that could tell us about dates, more than time, of course, I mean dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see that it is past the time for a break. I have very -- two very brief questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we are not there yet because we have sessions of one hour and we started late at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I have -- I'm almost done. I have few brief questions, if I may put them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, at the time of your work on the Srebrenica-related graves and the non-Srebrenica-related graves, was it possible to conduct a high volume of DNA analysis to identify the individuals?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Not really. In those dates, I mean, I wouldn't say DNA was at its infancy compared to what DNA or the use of DNA is now, but obviously no. Much progress has been done on -- on DNA testing very much in the last few years. In those days it was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And my final question to you is, then: The anthropological analysis of remains or the anthropological calculation of the minimum number of individuals or the minimum minimal number of individuals, were they -- are they still relevant in light of the DNA technology today?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Most definitely. Do remember DNA is - what would be the way to call it? - an additional or complementary technique that will be applied on the remains that will be used to calculate the minimal number of individuals, such as in this case. Just to clarify that, let's go back to the example I explained previously. We have a grave and we got lots of remains that are totally fragmented and we may have 50 right legs. My first idea would be to do DNA testing on those 50 right legs, so I will take a piece of each of them, pretty much as in a plane crash, for example, to establish that I got 50 DNA profiles with a specific sex as well, because as you do know now, unlike in previous occasions, the kits for DNA, to call them simply, contain a sex marker, amelogenin, the sex marker, and it will tell you whether it's an XX or an XY - a female or a male. So at least you know I have, I don't know, 49 males and one female. That is your base line. You will start working from then on. Another matter would be to reassociate the fragments, so you may say I do have at least 50 people, now the issue will be to reassociate the 50 and maybe I will find number 51, 52, 53 based on other fragments because the body, whatever, exploded or was burned beyond recognition or there were children and most of the bones burned down, and I will extract DNA from other bits and pieces. But definitely it's a complement. So the calculation of minimal number of individuals is totally -- it's a basic step, it's your first, I mean, step in any investigation of this nature. With or without DNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: This concludes my examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Lee. Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. You'll find him to your left. You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will go back to the last questions, trying to gain an explanation from you. The first thing I wanted to ask you is the methodology of calculation of MNI, of minimum number of individuals --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be a problem with the audio.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Can you increase the volume of this? Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you able to follow what Mr. Stojanovic said until now, Mr. Baraybar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you may then continue, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, the methodology you relied on to calculate the minimum number of individuals which you have discussed a moment ago is a generally accepted method, or did you adopt that method in the course of your work carried out for the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: It is -- it is a common or commonly accepted methodology. The specifics of the recording of all these body parts was obviously adapted to the type of case we were working. So the methodology as a whole is totally standard. The specifics of how you were encoding this or that and the type of forms you used were adapted to the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The methodology of calculation, as you present it here, of calculating the minimum number of individuals, is it a scientifically accepted method or was it something that you derived in the course of your work for the ICTY due to the specificities of the cases you encountered in the field?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: It is scientifically accepted. As I just repeat this to be very clear. The scientific method has been applied to all these calculations and therefore it is scientifically accepted. The specificity of recording is adapted to this but yet again following a scientific method. So the answer is yes, it is scientifically accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Between 1996 and 1999, were you conducting your work under the supervision of Dr. Wright and Dr. Haglund? Am I correct in assuming that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: In 1996, I was working with Dr. Haglund, yes, and under supervision of Dr. Haglund in 1996, yes. After 1996 it depend pretty much because when I was in the field I was under Dr. Wright, and when I was in the morgue I was working with the chief pathologist as the chief anthropologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any discussions and different approaches with regard to the method that was applied by Dr. Haglund, Dr. Wright, or other members of the team?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: There was always discussions. One of the most important things when looking back at those years is that there was a possibility of actually discussing and putting forward opinions and different experiences. Do remember that the teams were multi-national so there were people coming from other parts of the world with other experiences, and all the time there were discussions in that respect on how best to do things. Having said that, the final word was in the hand of the person who directed, I mean, the exhumation, be Professor Wright or Dr. Haglund at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Dr. Haglund exhibit any lack of understanding in that regard concerning the methodology you've discussed today?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, he had ideas regarding how to do things best. I would be -- I would say that, as the most important thing. As I said, every person has their own prerogatives. I mean, when I was in charge of an exhumation I had my own prerogative irrespective of what other people may think, so perhaps some people could think I was doing things in the wrong way but yet again I took my risk of doing them in that way because I thought I was right. So in that respect I would say that everybody has, I mean, their own ideas of how to do things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Such differences between your approach and that of Professor Haglund is something that I wanted to ask you further. Did it have any impact on the final outcome of choice of method in terms of calculating the minimum number of individuals and the lowest possible number of individuals?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, in terms of the methodology you applied to ascertain the age of the bodies, were there also different approaches or positions taken by you and Dr. Haglund?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, if I can recall, and I'm using only my memory here, in 1996, the -- there was a less standardised way of estimating age and grouping individuals into age classes. From 1997 onwards, and you have seen that on the various reports, we were using either four or three age groups to cluster people in. I -- as far as I recall in 1996, there was less of a grouping, and people were more, let's say, free to provide individual age intervals. So, for example, let me just explain this. While after 1997 we cluster individual examinations of bodies into groups, in 1996 there was no such grouping. So, for example, you say you got people between, I don't know, 13 and 16, and you got people from 15 to 18, and so on rather than saying this group of people would belong to the group 13 to 24, for example. But it's just a matter of order, of the way the data was arranged so, from 1997 onwards there was much more of a standard operating procedure, if you wish, in the way we reported the cases, also for those reading these reports, such as yourselves, as to be able to find information more quickly. In 1996 it was less order in that respect. It doesn't mean that it was badly done. It is just -- it means that it was a different way of doing things and there was no perspective of what would come in the future of course. I mean, there will be so many sites being dug up and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock, Mr. Stojanovic. I think it would be time for a break. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom? We take a break of 20 minutes, Mr. Baraybar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, good morning. If I could take an advantage of the interpreters briefly, Mr. Butler is ready but based on the time estimate, we shouldn't get to him today, and I don't -- so if we could -- if I could confirm with Mr. Stojanovic that we can give Mr. Butler a firm date for tomorrow, that would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from that, I do understand that Mr. Ivetic will cross-examine Mr. Butler and Mr. Ivetic will not arrive until tomorrow morning, is that well understood, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct, Your Honour. I will do my best to conclude with Mr. Baraybar today so that we can start with Mr. Butler tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If Mr. Butler would be on stand-by tomorrow morning, that would be okay. We take a break and we resume at 25 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Stojanovic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, we were discussing the method applied to determining the age of bodies. You told us that another age cluster or group was introduced in the reports following 1996. I wanted to ask you who it was that decided for an additional age group to be introduced in your tables in the reports?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Do remember that every individual, every set of remains that were ever analysed, be it 1996 or any other year afterwards, has its own age estimate. So you will prepare an age estimate for the remains you are analysing. After 1996, so beginning in 1997, for the sake of clarity for the Court, we clustered all those individual ages into age groups. So let's just distinguish the two things. I mean, one thing is individual age estimation on the remains, and something else is the way in which we presented information. So from 1997 onwards, it was my responsibility to present the reports with clustering of ages. It's just a matter of classification. So it's not something that is new, it's just the way in which information was presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That extra information, in terms of age, did it in any way correspond to the indictments which included boys and adults? Did such a change in methodology have anything to do with the texts of indictments in the Krstic or any other case?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, at the time, I hadn't read indictment so the answer is no. I mean, most definitely not. The cluster of ages has a logic within itself, and the logic is on the transition between boys or girls for that matter, I mean, young individuals from eight years of age up to age 12 or 13, then prepuberal, prepuberal individuals, meaning up to age more or less 15, and then teenagers as such, and then adults, that it would be a logical classification of that, that has nothing to do with any, I mean, indictment. I would do that in this case or any other case. It's just a biological transition so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would also like to ask you about the methodological approach you advocated in terms of defining the term "complete body." What in your view is the benchmark, the standard to be applied in that definition of a complete body?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I have to say that there was a debate regarding that and it is a very good question. In my opinion, a complete body would be at least one that had the head, had the thorax or the torso, and the legs. This body may be missing, for example, hands and feet may be missing, lower legs, and forearms, but the rest of it should be there to call it a complete body. Also because on such a quote/unquote complete body, you would be able to use multiple elements to estimate the age of the person. So, for example, it is highly unlikely you would be using the hands or the feet to estimate age according to the protocols that have been presented in the -- in the report, so at least you need the bulk of the body for it to be called a complete body.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was a uniform methodology adopted in defining complete bodies by those who worked on the exhumations between 1996 and 2001?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I would say that from 1997 onwards, there was a uniform or uniform criteria for the determination of a complete and incomplete bodies. In 1996 we are still working the making, so to speak. Do remember that was the first time in 1996 we were dealing with highly fragmented remains. Therefore, there was a bit of discussion regarding what would be a complete body or what would be a body part. But obviously body parts primarily refer to a leg, a foot, I mean, half a -- half a body, or things of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Before we move to the reports themselves, I wanted to ask you this: Having in mind your answer, Doctor, that to some extent you worked as an anthropologist whilst in another part of the exhumations as an archeologist, partly in the field as well as in the morgue as a professional, as an expert, were you present during the exhumations at Kasaba, Konjevic Polje, and Glogova?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I mean, in the specific -- let's see, in 1996, do remember there were some exhumations at Nova Kasaba and I was there, yes. Then in 1999 if I'm not mistaken - but yet again I'm using my memory here, not looking at the reports - there were the exhumations I conducted at Nova Kasaba again as well as Konjevic Polje and Glogova, but remember that Glogova, for example, has -- there is two Glogovas, 1 and 2. So Glogova 1, for example, I did not participate in that exhumation. I did actually on the other Glogovas that were across the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in the analysis of the Ravnice 1 grave-site on location?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Hmm, that's a tricky question. I do not recall. I believe I did not participate in the Ravnice 1 grave-site analysis, but I may -- I mean, I would need to check the documents, but I do not recall it frankly. What year was that? If you could be more precise with the year I could maybe tell you where I was then because I may have been at another site while the examination of the remains were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the report that was produced, the exhumation or, rather, analysis of the grave-site took place in 2000, in the course of 2000. That's what I find in your report. It was done on 2 February 2001.

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Is the report signed by me?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe so, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: If it is signed by me, I did it. But, I mean, since I don't have it in front of me, I'm just using my memory here. So if I signed it, I did it of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My goal is not to have it verified and confirmed. I believe I would be able to locate that piece of information. But let me be more specific: Can you recall which analyses of remains from primary and secondary graves did you carry out in the morgue rather than in the field?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I would rather refer to the reports. If you give me the chance to look at the reports, I would be able to tell you. But out of my own memory, I mean, I couldn't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the 2nd of February 2001 report, I think, is in evidence as P2088.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. And I will rely on the part referring to Ravnice, so we will deal with it that way. There is no need for me to explore it further.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the two grave-sites in Western Bosnia, Kevljani and Jakarina Kosa. Professor, do you recall having been present at the two locations?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. In the specific case of Kevljani, I was at the site perhaps during the first week of the exhumation. Then when bodies became available, I moved with them to the mortuary and I remained there for the duration of the time. And in the specific case of Jakarina Kosa, Jakarina Kosa was a site, if I'm not mistaken - yet again I'm using my memory here - that at the initial recovery of remains were started by the Bosnian Commission on Missing Persons and then the Tribunal took over the remains for them to be analysed. And, yes, I -- I took over and I pretty much conducted the analysis of those remains in Sanski Most. So I was present during the duration. I did visit the site of Jakarina Kosa, so I was shown the site where the remains were found by the investigators at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me this, Professor: Who specifically, according to the distribution of work, and I refer primarily to Eastern Bosnia exhumations, was in charge of securing the artefacts located in the graves or extracted from the graves?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Every team, be it field team or mortuary team, had a crime of scene officer. That was the person responsible for securing and maintaining the chain of custody of artefacts that were found outside the bodies, meaning in the grave fill. So, for example, if in a grave you found a number of bodies, maybe you would find elements within the grave fill, I mean in the dirt, I mean the shell casings, an ID card or something, not necessarily related to a specific body. In that case, we will request a number to that person and then a point would be taken to insert the location of that artifact within the map being prepared of the site. Then a picture would be taken, and then it would be handed over, this artefact would be handed over to a scene-of-crime-officer who would seal it in a bag, log it in a form, and then put it in a secure box to be transported later on to the Tribunal in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was a portion of those artefacts at some point destroyed as unnecessary?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That's something that should be asked to the evidence unit. I mean, I -- I do not know how many artefacts were kept or destroyed or -- or anything. I mean, that escapes me. That is nothing to do with my responsibility, not at the time or later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You did at no time make a decision or suggest which of the artefacts was to be deemed unnecessary and thus destroyed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, let me expand in this answer to be very clear. Let's start with the exhumation. At the exhumation site, you may find, for example, a shell casing, that would be deemed necessary since there is a number of things that can be done with a shell casing in terms of analysis. However, you would find a plastic bottle of water that contained no label, no brand, no evidentiary value in that respect, and those kind of things could be discarded. Or you would find, for example, a rusty can without any content, no label, whatsoever, so you would make just a note and you would just discard it. Now, once evidence was collected and was logged and stored, then it became the responsibility of the scene-of-crime officer and I personally or anybody else would have anything to say regarding what would happen to that evidence. Now, the second part of the -- of the answer would be, and that's something I did not mention in the previous question, is that bodies or body parts sometimes were clothed, I mean they have clothes on them, and within the clothes you would find still a number of artefacts, and those artefacts yet again will go through the same process. Meaning, they would be taken out of a pocket, for example, indicating from where they came from, so, for example, the upper left coat pocket, they would be photographed, they would be logged and stored. But also, for example, you would find things such as a small package with tobacco on it or an empty plastic bag, and those kind of things would be discarded making a note, of course, saying we found an empty bag in a pocket, but it has no evidentiary value. But remember, all decisions regarding evidence once it was in the hands of the evidence custodian was the prerogative of them. I mean, we had nothing to do then. We could only intervene at the recovery level. Making always a note, I mean not just simply discarding things but just saying I found a plastic bottle that says nothing so we will discard it. That's pretty much it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because I would like to complete this topic. Did you ever hear objections voiced by many victims associations with regard to the fact that many of the artefacts that had been discovered in those graves had in the meantime been destroyed? Have you heard any such objections with regard to your work?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, I haven't, and as a matter of fact the only allegation that comes to my memory is not related to this case, not to a case being dealt with formally by the Tribunal, and it regards actually an investigation in Albania we carried out while heading the office of missing persons regarding some medical elements or medicines that were found on a site in Albania that were then destroyed. I mean, as far as I know that was all over the press at some point in time. That is what I do know. But I mean regarding this other case or this specific case, I haven't heard about it. Also I confess that I have not been following the news very carefully to see what allegations were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Let's look at P2086. I'm interested in page 3, both in English and B/C/S. Professor, this is your report. If the Prosecutor agrees, I don't have a problem if you want to look at it in the hard copy because I know that you have it with you. So this is your report from August and October 1999. This has already been admitted. Please help us and explain some things for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, and we are talking about Nova Kasaba 4. I hope you were able to locate the page. We are still talking about the methodology with regard to determining the age of the bodies that were exhumed. Can we continue, Professor? Are you okay? In paragraph 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which would be, Your Honours, Nova Kasaba 4, the second paragraph from the bottom, both in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In that paragraph, you say that the bodies of 19 adult males were found in the grave, two of them had a mean age of 17 years at the time of death. Now, we are talking about two bodies with the average age of 17. Could one then say that one of them was 14 and that the other one was 20? Could you please try and explain, based on the methodology that you used and that you have already addressed during your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I believe that it is much more a matter of the way it is written. I mean, the report has been written in a manner to make it easy to understand. The specific ages would need to be traced back to the specific forms, autopsy forms of each one of the cases to see what was the specific age range given to them. Obviously, it would be too cumbersome to include information of that kind into a report like this one, but it is just a matter of form more than of content, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: However, was the age of those individuals determined individually? How did you arrive at that mean age? If I look at the method that you used when it comes to determining the age, and I'm referring to the table that we subsequently received, and there are age groups, there is an age group distribution there.

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just be more detailed regarding this. Whenever you estimate age on a set of remains, whether they be complete or incomplete, you would have an interval between two numbers, a range, okay? Because we estimate biological age, not chronological age. I mean, all of us have a chronological age since we were born on a specific date, and if you have an ID card you would say you're 48 or almost 49 years or whatever or 48 and 11 months. But when you have remains, you have to establish two parameters, so saying this person cannot be younger than so much nor older than so much. And between these two numbers you can establish the mean, an arithmetic mean, and say, for example, you are 17 years of age plus/minus, right, a given amount to tell you you are, for example, between, I don't know, 14 and 20. Your mean would be 17. But it means in reality that you could be 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20. That is -- that is the way it is -- it is done. So, yes, every individual has been aged individually, if even I'm being redundant here, but then when reporting the ages as a whole, as a group, we have been placing those individual ages into groups just to simplify reading or understanding the distribution of the ages. But, for example, let's assume that this clustering or distribution of ages, it is complicated to understand, we do not like it or whatever, we can always refer back to the specific autopsy reports. The problem is if I reported that in such a way, it would be impossible to read. It would say, for example, we found 19 people. Individual number 1 was between 14 and 20. Individual number 2 was between 15 and 23. Individual number 3 and so on. So it would be very cumbersome to read. So it's two different things: One is the individual assessment of age that exists for every single case we have done from 1996 onwards, and the way you use that estimate to present it in a cluster. They are two different things. So to answer your question, yes, the age has been estimated individually. The way it has been reported on the reports is different but that's just a matter of -- of presentation, not of content. I don't know if I have explained myself, Counsellor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for my benefit, can you expand on the table? When it comes to such an approach in the method of entering data into the tables, was that approach generally accepted? Or let me put it the other way: There are tables where we find the remains of the bodies of 12 year old boys. Would it be possible for such tables to contain data on the bodies of individuals aged 12 and aged 20, for example, so they do not fit into the mean that you presented in your report separately?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Actually, no. All it means is that the category, for example, between 8 and 12, it means that the person most definitely is not younger than eight, okay? However, it is very possible that somebody that was classified in the next category, okay? 13 to 17 or 15 or whatever, could be part of this younger age and vice versa. Having said that, there is another -- another element that is very important. The age categories to cluster individuals in these groups, okay, have been defined using some specific markers, meaning, for example, in the category 8 to 12, the pelvis, the pelvic bones, were still separated into pieces meaning they have not fused, and we know that it is normal that across populations, about -- about age 12, they are fused. But if you find it in two pieces, you knew that this person was not 12 because normally it is typical that somebody who is much younger than 12 would have these pieces separated. By the same token, we could say, for example, that if the second molar bone, you know that adults have three molar bone, the second molar bones, if you look at the crown of the -- of the tooth, the crown was completed by the root because you know that teeth grow from above to below. First you have the crown and then you have the root. It is in reverse of what we really think. I mean it's not coming from below to above but above to below. So when you have the root, for example, to one-quarter, if you get one-quarter of the root, you do know that this person is about, yet again, 12 years of age. But if the root would be, let's say, smaller, and in addition to that, if the case is complete, you would have the pelvic bone in two pieces, you would know this person is not 12. It is younger than 12. So yet again, every -- every age cluster or group is categorised by markers. So it was not only an issue of saying I have this individual here between whatever, 9 and 12, and then because I want so I will put it into the category 8 to 12. I would need to check as well that that age estimation is in accordance --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, please. I apologise for interrupting. I'm -- it may be my mistake for asking such complicated questions, but let's finish this. In this report you say that there were two bodies in Nova Kasaba 4 grave whose mean age is 17. Would I be right or would you be right to say that these two bodies belonged to individuals who were aged between 12 and 20 because I am attaching that information to those age clusters that you presented in your tables, i.e. it cannot happen that one body from one age group entered that mean of 17 years of age, actually skipped the table or went from one table group to another table group and found himself in a wrong table group, "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The possibility of classifying one individual that had the border or the transition between groups to one side or the other is always possible. So the answer in that respect will be yes. However, having said that, regard to your specific question that I'm reading here, you asked me whether these individuals that have a mean age of 17 could be in the range between 12 and 20, yes, they could, but to see that and to tell you yes to that, I would need to see the specific autopsy reports of those cases that I do not have in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Professor. And now look at the last sentence on this page. According to the pathologists report, two of them died of multiple gunshot wounds other than the dressed ones, whereas the cause of death was not established for eight of them. Within the context of this report, what are firearms? Are we talking about gunshot wounds, blast wounds, wounds inflicted by explosives or mines, or are we talking only about small weapons or infantry weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Okay. Just to make sure that we are looking at the same page, if it's Nova Kasaba 4, it says here: "According to the pathologist's report, 11 died of gunshot wounds while the cause of death of the eight others was unascertained." You mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should look at the last two lines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies. Right. But that refers to something very specific. So let's see. It refers to individuals that have dressings. It says here: "Three individuals showed dressings and a splint and may have been injured prior to the disposal to the grave because they had dressings," and normally would you dress a wound of somebody that was alive, I mean, in principle. "According to the pathologist's report, two of them, two of the three that had dressings, died of multiple gunshot wounds other than the dressed ones." So I do recall, for example, there was one individual that have a dressing on the lower leg, if I'm not mistaken where there was a perforating -- or a through-and-through, rather, wound through the tibia to the shin bone, but this person sustained gunshot injuries to the head and the cause of death was determined as gunshot wound to the head. Obviously it means that this person survived the injury to the lower leg because it had a dressing and the death came after. I mean, how long after we do not know. Obviously it was not years after because, I mean, there was still a dressing. When we refer to gunshot wounds, primarily most -- in most of the cases with very few exceptions, and I cannot recall any exception at this moment, when we refer to gunshot wounds they were caused primarily by the same type of ammunition, and we found in many cases, I mean, the shells and the -- and the bullets themselves that were 7.62 by 51 millimetres, pretty much AK 47 family ammunition. Whenever we found shrapnel, it was indicated that the injuries were caused which shrapnel. They were not indicated as gunshot wounds. So gunshot wounds primarily referred to wounds caused by in this case by generally 7.62 by 51 millimetres ammunition, so a rifle ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I was waiting for the interpretation to finish. I apologise. Your answer to my question was only partial. When you say in the report that the injuries were caused by firearms, that they were gunshot wounds, do you imply only infantry weapons or rifles or do you also imply other types of weaponry and artillery weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Remember that in bones, the characteristics of gunshot wounds are very well known and there is a correlation that between certain calibres of weapon and the gunshot wounds in bone, okay, so you would have -- you could classify roughly the relationship between the gunshot wound, I mean the hole on the bone and the calibre of the weapon, into three groups. Very low calibres, like 0.22, for example, that would leave a very small hole, that would be similar, slightly below the 0.22 of an inch in this case. You got another group where you can classify handguns of the group 0.38 and 9 millimetres that yet again will create a slightly bigger hole, that it would be between 0.38 of an inch and 9 millimetres approximately, and then you have also the group of the high velocity rounds that yet again divides itself into two because you have the 5.56 and the 7.62 millimetres for those two. But in those cases, it depends pretty much to know whether the bullet entered in this case the bone perpendicular, so to leave a round hole, or it entered in a different way. So, for example, we have a number of cases that we have reported, as a matter of fact, where bullets entered the body sideways, and by doing that they left a hole, they punched a hole that is the equivalent of the bullet on a side view. So you could actually measure, I mean, a triangular hole and you could take the bullet and put it there and it is the same. So in those cases you could say this individual was shot by a rifle or this individual was likely shot by a handgun. So that is the way it has been done. Now, I wouldn't like to go into details of whether it's infantry ammunition or not because I mean I'm not a military expert on that respect, but whenever it was possible to say this individual was shot by a rifle or by a handgun, it was definitely said. In the majority of cases, the ammunition found in some cases under the body where people were shot in the grave, for example, you have the body, you got, for example, a gunshot wound to the head, and then you lifted the head and underneath a bit of soil you could find a slug of the ammunition that shot him was a rifle ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Taking into account your answer, and bearing in mind that this is a pathologist's report, and I asked you about the places that you were present at yourself and the others where you wrote reports in the morgue, are you able to answer as to what weapons were used to inflict those mortal wounds in these individuals? Are you able to answer that question or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I -- I believe you refer to specific case Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Nova Kasaba 4. Professor, I will go from one place to the next, and we will deal about the very specific location of all the bullets. When it comes to Kasaba 4, would it be correct that as an anthropologist you cannot tell us what weapons were used to inflict mortal wounds in these 11 individuals, "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: As I said before, I have been using the information provided to me by the pathologists since I worked on the recovery of those remains and not on the analysis of the remains, so the answer in that context would be no. But you should refer for that matter to the pathologist's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I'm going to ask you something else. Let's move on to the following page, both in B/C/S -- no, no, let's stick to the B/C/S page that is on the screen, but we need the following page in English. Professor, you've already commented on this page, and you mentioned some specific cases in Nova Kasaba 4, you told us that there were traces of dressings and other medical material used on those wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now, Your Honours, in the same document I would like to look at page 11 in English and this is the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And after saying or rather commenting upon Nova Kasaba 4 report, you say in the last paragraph a possible cloth ligature was found loose in the grave fill. However, no evidence of individuals tied or blindfolded was found. Based on your experience with ligatures and their existence, and based on your specific experience with the graveyards in Nova Kasaba and Konjevic Polje that are dealt with in this report, did you deal with that in your analysis and did you refer to that in your report?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I do not understand the question. I mean, if I dealt with what exactly? With the ligatures? Meaning, did I analyse the ligatures? Or -- if you could clarify, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In very specific terms, maybe I was too general in my previous question so I'll try to rephrase it. Was your task at any point in time to analyse the existence of ligatures and blindfolds, if you were to find those in the graveyards, were you supposed to analyse them in any way?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Not -- not the anthropologist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, the evidence in this case has been that these were mass graves, and perhaps it's a translation issue, but these mass graves have been identified as graveyards, and those are two separate words. And this is just to clarify for the record, because that has not been the evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think we are talking in this context about graves which contained a large number of bodily remains which is usually not referred to as a graveyard. Maybe a translation issue. May I take it that you understood the question to be about the graves and could you answer the question if you would find ligatures and blindfolds whether you were supposed to analyse them in any way? I think you answered that question that you were not supposed to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have moved a step ahead based on Judge Orie's question. Would I be correct in saying that according to the report, in the grave-sites of Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje, and Glogova 2, you did not come across ligatures and blindfolds or anything that would have any association with those?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Since your question referred only to one site, Nova Kasaba 4 if I am not mistaken, I answered that we found the ligatures, as it said in the report, loose in the grave, and I also answered that the anthropologist was not in charge of analysing the ligature itself. That was the prerogative of the scene-of-crime officer that would collect and photograph and describe that element. However, in the other sites, you know, I could not tell you if I found that "yes" or "no" unless, of course, I went through every report and tell you what's in the reports. I do not remember by heart whether I found ligatures or not in all the other sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, we'll go through most of those you worked on. Now that you mentioned the bandaging that was found, would that bandage correspond to something you referred to in your report on page 12, where you say that something that reminds of ligature was found, a piece of cloth?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The dressing -- I mean, let's see if I understand you correctly. In that report, and there is a picture on it, there is a leg with a dressing, meaning a patch of cloth secured with some bandages, if you wish to call it, or bandaged leg, with a square padded piece of cloth and with some pieces of branches, of tree branches that were running parallel to the leg and were also fixed to this compound of cloth and everything, and that for me is a dressing. Now, when I refer to possible ligatures, and I'm using the word "possible," I'm not affirming it, is some piece of cloth that has or is shaped as a number 8 where you got two round elements as those used to put the wrist of somebody. Since we have seen so many proper ligatures on the bodies of many cases, I could infer that this piece of cloth shaped in such a way was a ligature. But since I did not find a ligature on a body, I say it's possible ligature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, did you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction:

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you at any time informed of the route taken by the 28th Division column on their attempt of breakthrough from Srebrenica to Tuzla? And can you tell us whether you estimated the distance between the breakthrough route and the specific grave-site location Nova Kasaba 4?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No. I was not informed of those specifics. I do know in general terms that that area was a crossing area based pretty much on the literature I read at the time regarding what had happened in those -- in those days, at least as interpreted by the people writing the books, but I have never been given specific information regarding people, you know, were I don't know how many metres away and this and that. We were never let's say fed the very specifics of the -- of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As you said during examination-in-chief, you could not establish the time of death of the 19th persons found in the Nova Kasaba 4 grave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Also, based on the information you have, specifically concerning Nova Kasaba 4, you could not tell whether they were killed in the grave, on the grave-site, or if they were killed elsewhere and then buried at that location.

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Let me please check the report to see whether that is correct or not. I mean, I would need to go through the pages. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Page 3 and 4 in the English version of the document, Professor. The explanation pertaining to the image can be found on page 11 and 12.

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: If there is no mention in the report of slugs found under the bodies, we cannot affirm specifically that people may have been shot while in the grave. So any time that we found the slugs of the bullets under the bodies, under some soil, of course, we could say these people were shot while in the grave. If that information is not specified in the report, it means we have not been able to determine such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was my presumption as well. We will come across some similar situations still. For the time being, let's look at page 4 in the B/C/S and page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, before you continue, I'm a bit confused. I think your question was about people being killed in the grave and then you said on the grave-site. Or if they were killed elsewhere and then buried at that location. I understood that question to be whether they were killed in the -- in or in the immediate vicinity of where they were buried or that they were transported over a longer distance to that grave. I don't know where you draw the line, but I would consider that to be more than, well, let's say 100 or 200 metres, so further away from the grave-site. Now, the answer of the witness very much focused on being shot in the grave itself. So therefore, your question does not fully match with the answer. And when you then said that was my presumption as well, I was confused whether it was the presumption or what you dealt with in your question, or whether it was what the witness dealt with in his answer, which, again, was not fully congruent. I am looking at the clock. We will take a break and the witness could already be escorted out of the courtroom, but I would also like to read a decision when the witness is -- has left the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The decision I would like to deliver on behalf of the Chamber is the Chamber's decision with regard to the Defence notice objection and motion to bar Witness Richard Higgs from testifying as an expert, a motion which was filed on 19th of December, 2012. The Prosecution responded on the 31st of December. As for the applicable law concerning expert evidence, the Chamber refers to its decision concerning Richard Butler, filed on the 19th of October, 2012. The Defence argue that is Witness Higgs is not an expert and should therefore not be allowed to present expert evidence before the Chamber. The witness's CV and the submissions by the Prosecution indicate that the witness has completed relevant training and has extensive working experience in the field of mortar weaponry. In particular, the witness worked as a mortar operations and project manager in the British army for 15 years. The witness also acted as a United Nations mortar consultant for two years. On this basis, the Chamber is satisfied that the witness is a mortar weaponry expert who can assist the Chamber on matters related to the shelling incidents charged in the indictment. As for any arguments related to the methodology of the Higgs report, the Chamber considers that these are matters that can be and should be addressed during the examination of the witness. Finally, with regards to the Defence request to cross-examine the witness, the Chamber notes that the witness will be called to testify and the Defence will therefore have the opportunity to cross-examine him. Based on the foregoing, the Chamber decides that Witness Higgs may testify as an expert witness and denies the Defence request to bar the Prosecution from presenting his evidence. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. Before we take the break, I would take a bit of a longer break than usual and then continue for another 75 minutes after the break. That would be to take a break of half an hour to resume at 1.00 and then to finish at quarter past 2.00, if this would not be objected to, and I see Mr. Stojanovic you are not objecting to such a schedule. We take a break and we'll resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness will be escorted into the courtroom. As matters stand now, Ms. Lee, do you know how much time you would need for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: I have none so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: None so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Baraybar. Mr. Stojanovic will now continue his cross-examination. You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, we have dealt with a dilemma concerning the place of death of those found in Nova Kasaba 4. It concerns the 19th bodies of adult males. I wanted to ask you something with regard to your last answer. You cannot state, based on the scientific analysis and rules of your profession, whether it was possible that the bodies had been collected elsewhere and then buried in that grave, and also that before the bodies were buried they had spent a certain amount of time on the ground as surface remains?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The second part of your question is something I cannot affirm primarily because we did not find any indication of advanced decomposition prior to the bodies being buried. Normally, a body left on the surface would be infested by fly eggs, they would become maggots and then in turn they would become pupae of flies and then the flies would come from there. So we did not find any such body as we did find in some other cases, though, where they were pretty much infested with larvae indicating that it had been sometime or they were sometimes left on the surface. That's one issue. As a second issue, that is the first part of your question, I have only stated in the reports whenever I found slugs under the bodies that were matching with injuries that the person was likely shot on the grave. This does not exclude, however, that people could have been shot next to the grave or 2 metres away from it or whatever. That's something I cannot affirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we together look at P2086 again, page 4 in both versions. We are still -- or actually we are discussing the grave-site Nova Kasaba 7. In this example you are referring to cartridges found in the grave. Let me clear something up first. According to the report, the remains of one person were found there, the person being an adult male between 31 and 65 years of age. Would it be correct to say that if there was only one body, it could not be seen as a mass grave according to the standards you adopted?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It was not a mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And in your view, what is to be understood under the term "mass grave"?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Technically, it's a grave that contains more than one person. I mean, there have been some classifications, most of them useless, as a matter of fact, between individual multiple and mass, but that is totally arbitrary. What you do have as a matter of fact is individual graves is one person, and then mass graves or multiple graves, whatever definition you want to choose, that contain more than one individual. There is no fact to establish that if you have five people, seven people, it becomes something else. I mean, whether you have one person or whether you have many people, so, for me at least to my standard, you have a mass grave as one having more than one person. Another one would be a grave, a single grave, as in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this case, it is stated that evidence confirms that the person was shot in the grave itself. You go on to say that large calibre ammunition shell casings were found of 30 millimetre calibre. That, together with the fact that only one body was disposed therein suggested that the trench was originally used as a gun emplacement. Let me ask you this: Such 30-millimetre shell casings as found in this grave, were they the basis of your conclusion that the person was fired at whilst in the grave?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Most definitely not. Actually, if we look at the -- I mean, this is a summary of the report, so if you look at the report itself, there are a few pages after, you can see that this grave was kind of an opportunistic grave-site, meaning the body was lying on some sediment or some dirt that has been used to backfill this hole, and then the body was added to that. In addition to this 30-millimetre ammunition, that obviously is something with which you would not shoot somebody, I mean at least at close range because there would not be any body left, is what made us assume or interpret this hole as a gun emplacement. However, there was a rifle ammunition that was found also next to the body, meaning shell casings in this case, and perhaps a slug if I'm not mistaken, and even -- I mean, I would need to check the report again, I was reading the report during the break, I think there is small hand gun ammunition as well, perhaps 7.65 millimetres, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We can look together at page 17, or, rather, page 17 in the English version, where you refer to it. It is the last paragraph. As well as the penultimate paragraph of page 16 in the English. Since we are on that topic, I wanted to discuss some details with you. Let us wait first. Thank you. Your Honours, I would like to direct your attention to the penultimate and ultimate paragraph. There you say the following: "At the feet of the body, a number of bullets and shell casings were found. There were three 7.62-millimetre shell casings, two 7.62-millimetre bullets, one bullet jacket fragment, and a 7.65-millimetre pistol bullet." Let me ask you this first: Three 7.62-millimetre shell casings were found in the grave. There were no slugs in the grave itself corresponding to the casings calibre, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, there were two slugs. I mean two 7.62 millimetre bullets, meaning the slugs. So you got three shell casings, two slugs, and one jacket fragment, according to what the report says.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, perhaps I needn't go into the field of ballistics but maybe it is a matter of translation. In my understanding a casing is the part of a bullet containing the primer, powder charge, and the bullet itself, the slug. In my understanding, you found three such casings, i.e., jacket fragments, and then you say bullets. Is it a bullet which had not been spent, including both a slug, a primer, and a gunpowder, or are all these just parts of something that we refer to as slugs?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Your question is totally pertinent. I believe, and I'm doubting myself now, we got three casings, meaning the shell case, right, the area where the powder would go and the primer, what I'm doubting now, and that's something I cannot confirm yet again, whether it's an issue of the way I've written it, but you may be right that we are talking about two bullets - meaning complete bullets, meaning the slug and the casing - meaning unspent cartridges, that would be another way to put it, and one jacket fragment. So you may be right in what I'm saying, but I cannot affirm or deny it, I mean, at the moment based on this report, but you my be right. I would need to see whether I have used the term "bullet" and when I've used the term "slug" in previous cases. But it says bullet, it is very likely, as you said, that they're unfired ammunition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question and the answer raise an issue of what exactly a slug means and what exactly a bullet means, whether the bullet is just the projectile which leaves the cartridge after the cartridge being ignited or whether it means cartridge plus bullet still in place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm just checking, Your Honour, further on the report, to see whether it's a matter of semantics or to what I'm referring exactly. If you give me one second, I will confirm it to you in a second. As a matter of fact, across the report, I have been using the term "bullet." In this case I do refer to "slug," but technically it is totally right to affirm that a bullet would need to be referred as an unspent cartridge or an unfired cartridge in this case containing the shell case and the bullet itself. However, in other parts of the report I've been referring to bullets as being found under the bodies and matching the injuries that the body sustained by gunshot; i.e., meaning, that I'm referring to it to a slug. But I would -- I would concur that looking at this now, it is an incorrect use of the term. However, in some other parts of the report I've been using unspent ammunition as referring to the whole bullet meaning that it has not been fired, as if the bullet itself with the shell casing and the slug was simply found in association to remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I will continue with the last paragraph of page 17. In this specific case, you say that no -- well, casing or slug, whatever it may be, correspond with the position of the body itself, and that it was not found underneath the body itself. Would I be correct, then, in concluding that the assertion of this person being fired at in the grave was merely an assumption, not an assertion?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. If you read the language in which the report has been written, it's all in conditional. Obviously, the body was found in a part of the grave. I can't remember what corner it was found but it was found on a -- on part of the grave. And unlike previous cases, the slugs in this case, not the case in the slugs, were not directly under the body, okay, as we have found before. This does not, however, exclude the fact that the person could have been shot while in the grave and then pushed, for example, but everything is put in conditional because we do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you confirm that in this specific case, based on the rules of your profession, you could not ascertain the time of death of this person?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Let us go back to page 4 again, please, in both versions. I'd like to discuss the Nova Kasaba 8 grave-site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, could I ask clarification on one issue. You say you conclude that someone is shot in a grave when a bullet, I mean the projectile or the slug, as you call it, is found under the body. Would you agree with me that if you shoot someone who is already in a grave but still alive, that there is a fair chance that the bullet by which you kill that person may well be found next to the body or not necessarily to be under the body itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends. For example, if I shoot somebody through the chest considering that the chest is quite large as compared to the arm, for example, it is likely the slug would be under the body. Now, in some instances, and it is also written in the report, you have migration of slugs, meaning that the slug remain in the soft tissues, the soft tissues decay, and the slug was found a bit further, you know, away from the body. That is totally possible. Primarily when you have bodies superimposed to one another, so you've got many bodies one on top of the other, the slug of one on top could end up on the bottom. That is totally possible. But in areas of the body that are quite large, you actually do find the slug underneath it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if someone is killed by being hit by a bullet which hit but, well, for example let's say an artery in the arm or something like that leading to bleeding to death, you might well find the bullet at a distance of 2 metres from that body.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The cartridge, not the slug, meaning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, if a -- if the projectile itself --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the thing that flies and that pierces the body part, for example, an arm, which is still possible, it would exit the body with still some energy and may move or travel until the edge of the grave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you're not lying down against the floor. If you're standing, of course, or sitting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- or whatever, certainly in that context, yes. When I refer people being shot, it is that lying. Obviously lying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I understand you better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because being in a grave and lying in a grave may not be the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now look the part that refers to the Nova Kasaba 8 graveyard, Professor. In the summary you say that a total of 33 persons were found there and for one person it was impossible to establish the gender. Bearing in mind everything that you've already said with regard to the way a person's sex may be determined, how come that you couldn't determine the sex of that particular person? Why?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: We would need to refer to the specific autopsy report of that case. I mean, yet again I cannot answer the question without having the report. It could be that the remains were in very poor preservation or state of preservation, that none of the elements used for sex determination would be found, but I would need to have the report in front of me to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
