utterances.text: Help us, please, and try and remember who was the pathologist who worked on the Nova Kasaba grave sites?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you frankly. I mean, those specifics, I mean, escape me completely. I mean, I do -- I would need to know who was the person who looked at the remains, who was the anthropologist, what is present in the anthropological forms, and then be able to tell you the explanation is because, I don't know, the body was broken or was very decomposed and the bones were decomposed as well. I mean, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, those last questions, what are they telling us? I mean, what should the Chamber understand from not knowing exactly why the gender could not be determined? I mean, what -- what could we learn from it, relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as I was preparing to cross-examine Mr. Baraybar, I could see that the methodology that was used in determining the gender was not reliable at the time, and this is precisely one of the arguments that we already discussed, hence my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't remember that reliability of the methodology was questioned. I mean I would be very much interested to hear questions about that, but none of those questions was put to the witness, as far as I remember. At least not today. And I really would be interested, rather than to have a kind of vague question about would you know why it could not be established. If it's unreliable, put questions to the witness. Put to him what makes the method used unreliable, whether the pelvic bone is not an indication whatsoever or whatever it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honour. Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, during the examination-in-chief, you did talk about the criteria used to determine gender. In your written report and earlier today you said that it was relatively easy if there was still some soft tissue left. If however there was no soft tissue but only skeletal remains, you also mentioned what the criteria were. Would it be right to conclude that for that reason when there was no soft tissue left, the body is so fragmented that you cannot ascertain the person's gender with any degree of certainty?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Not really. I mean, the answer will be not always. Obviously we have a foot or if you have a hand, your reliability in sex determination will be very low. But if you have for example a leg, you will be much better off than if you have a hand or a foot alone. Needless to say, if you have a complete body or half a body. So reliability decreases with the amount, so to speak, and the key areas of the body that are normally used to sex a skeleton. We understand that in an ideal world, having a complete body, you would look at the pelvis first, there's a number of characteristics in the pelvis. Then you would use a skull, and then you would use the long bones. But remember as well that you have two options to go around this: I mean, one of them is morphological, so you're going to look at the shape and proportions of various areas of those bones; and the other one is metrical, so you can always measure certain bones or certain bone parts and either apply some charts that may have been derived from that or other populations that will give you some idea as to whether to ascribe these remains or not. And this is very important because as you indicated, whenever a body had soft tissue and had external genitalia, obviously you would establish the sex as being male or female because you're looking at it. When not having soft tissues, you would need to look at whatever was present, but one may say that sexing of body parts has been very unreliable, but I can tell you that that was not the case, because in one of the Konjevic Polje sites, we did find a female and this is a bit of an anecdote -- an anecdote, but it's important to say it, is that we were so used to finding males, skeletally speaking, that when there was this female found, I had to pull the body out of the freezer to be convinced that it was actually a female because I remember that I step out of the excavation for a moment and this body was pulled out, and one of my staff told me, by the way, we just found a female. And I said, "No, it's not possible. There is no females here. We've been seeing men all throughout. Just take the body out." The body was taken out and with a cursory examination on the spot, I said, "You're right. It is a female." So all I'm trying to say is that by no means I think we been or the sex estimation in this case has been lets say unreliable. Obviously there is a large percentage of cases that have been sexed as undetermined because we didn't have any elements to provide I mean, you know, sex estimation on those cases. So no -- nor we have been sexing everybody as males nor as females nor as undetermined, and obviously the number of undetermined is quite large as you can imagine because there were body parts that could not be examined towards a sex estimation because there were hands, feet, or very fragmented pieces of bodies that didn't yield any kind of information of such kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now let's look at data for Nova Kasaba 8. In the summary you say that a total of 33 persons were found there. You also say that they were buried in three different groups. What I would like to know is this: If we are looking at the appearance of the Nova Kasaba 8 grave, right, were you -- were they buried next to each other or on top of each other?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: It may be -- it may be good to look at the picture of this grave of Nova Kasaba 8 to answer the question on page 20 of the English report. In Nova Kasaba 8, what you see are three groups of people that are superimposed on one another. The way we excavated the grave and take the pictures you have on the report shows like steps, like three steps. These three steps represents three groups of people that have been buried in different moments. By moments I mean I cannot calculate whether it was a matter of hours, days, I mean I obviously cannot estimate that, but it's a time or relative time difference between one group and the other. So group number 1 is the one that's pretty much at the bottom, the first one to have been placed, these are a group of people that have been just thrown in there, and then group number 2, as I come, the step of the middle, and group number 3 is the last group of bodies to have been placed on this -- on this grave, so the body have been pretty much, yes, thrown in -- in clusters, together.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please pay attention to the last paragraph where you say, leaves and branches of willow trees found on the bodies in group 1 could link them to Nova Kasaba 05, I can't call this a grave for understandable reason, as a possible place of execution. How did you identify Nova Kasaba 5 if no buried bodies were found there? What made you identify it as a possible execution or burial site?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. In the photograph that was shown to us by the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just for clarity, P2087 is what we should perhaps look at at this moment. Maybe we would get a clearer picture on the whole area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that photograph, there is an aerial -- an aerial image. What you see -- ah, there you go. What you can see from above, so to speak, are some white or lighter areas with various shapes. Some of them have no specific shapes and some of them are like rectangular and so on. The area of the circle of NAK-05 was seen from above, yet again, as a lighter area. The assumption at the time was that it was a grave because it is shaped as a rectangle and we thought that was a grave. And we went to dig it up. And we opened some trenches across. It was not a grave. It was literally a scrape of the surface with a machine, obviously, with the blade of a machine like, for example, a front end loader. You know, a scrape. So from the air what you see it's the same thing as the other areas that were proven to be graves. Now, if you look at the picture very closely, to the left of the picture, you would see on an oblique angle a small roundish or elongated area of also lighter soil. Well, that is a small mound of dirt next to a willow tree or, rather, in the middle of the mound there is a willow tree. And you see also that the rectangular area -- and this little mound is connected by two tracks, what proved there was a mechanised machine that actually was doing something there. Now, that willow tree was the only willow tree of the whole area you are seeing on the photograph. We took the time to walk around the whole area looking for willow trees and there was no other willow trees. So branches of willow were found in cluster 1 at the site at Nova Kasaba 8, and in the mound in Nova Kasaba 5 - that is, next to the willow tree - there were some shell casings, okay? So the assumption or, rather, the interpretation of these facts is the following: If people could have been shot on that spot, the bodies would have been collected or taken by a bladed machine such as a front end loader, the front end loader in the path of collecting and pushing would have gone all the way to the willow tree as the tracks are indicating, shaking the willow trees, and having some willow branches on the bodies that would have been transported to the first cluster of Nova Kasaba 8. In other words, there is no other logical explanation to explain why branches of willow tree, not leaves but branches, would have ended up among the bodies of cluster number 1 in Nova Kasaba 8. So the interpretation of these findings was that one. There is a plausible and a logical interpretation based on these findings. Of course, if there were willow trees all over the place, I could not affirm such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber in view of the fact that you were there on the spot, what is the distance between Nova Kasaba 5 and the Nova Kasaba 8 graveyard?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Hmm, that's a tricky question. I wouldn't know. My guess, but it's just a guess, would be perhaps 100 metres, considering the width of the road, perhaps 100 metres, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is there a single explanation which arises from the rules of your profession for the fact that a hole was dug at the Nova Kasaba 5 locality for the people to be executed there and driven a distance of 100 metres to the place where they would be buried in the place that we later on marked as Nova Kasaba 8?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: There may be some confusion here. Nova Kasaba 5 is not a grave. There's no hole. It is not a hole. It's just a scraping of the surface. What you see from above is just an area of light -- light soil, but it is not a hole. It is just a scrape of the turf of the grass of the surface. Obviously from below what we thought when we saw the picture is you have another grave there, but in order to prove that it was not a grave, we trenched it, we opened some trenches across, some excavations across, and could you see that it was natural soil. So there has never been a hole there, it was just a scrape of the surface. Now, why would people use that area and then move the bodies elsewhere, I do not know. What I can infer based on pure logic of the findings is that the only willow tree was found in that area and some willow branches, that I'm not affirming, are the specific willow branches from that willow tree, because I haven't done DNA for that, were found in the cluster 1 on Nova Kasaba 8. So it is a logical inference is what I'm trying to say. The reason why, I mean, that's obviously escapes me and it would not be in my realm of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask a question, Mr. Baraybar. You explained a few minutes ago that between the big white area on NK-05 and the willow tree, there are tracks which you explained a few minutes ago as possibly the blade of a front end loader. I see when I look at the top part of that same big white area of NK-05, something similar to those tracks coming round on the right side of that white, going right down NK-08. Can you see that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to comments on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is definitely possible that those tracks leading from NK-05 to NK-06 are definitely related to the event that we are looking at as NK-05.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But they go past down to NK-08.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is correct. I mean, remember as well that there is a number of tracks in that -- in that area, because we have already established that some of the graves, including NK-08, were created by a front end loader, so obviously a front end loader was operating in the area. That's something we can -- we can infer. There is no doubt, for example, in the area of NK-08 that there was a machine excavated grave that the bucket of the machine, of the front end loader in this case has some teeth because the teeth marks were found in the soil, so could -- I mean, there is a machine operating in the area and those tracks could be the link -- could be the link as well between NK-05 and NK-08.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In relation to the question by Mr. Stojanovic that is it possible or is it possible that bodies could be transported 100 metres down from NK-05 to NK-08 for burial after being killed there, what would that indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Obviously my opinion would be slightly beyond the scope of my own profession, but I could say that NK-05 is a site that the is literally next to the road. Next -- I mean, a couple of metres away from the road, while the other sites are -- that are the proper graves, NK-06, 8, and 4 are proper graves. NK-07 is just an opportunistic grave in my opinion, was being used as something else and they just put a body inside. Obviously, the idea would be to move bodies away from the road. You could -- you could -- you could for the sake of argument you could say that the issue of concealing bodies in this case would be to conceal them away from the road or to dispose them away from the road if the word "concealment" sounds too interpretive in this -- in this case, but definitely NK-05 is next to the road, and if you had bodies next to the road, perhaps you wanted to move them away from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now another question about Nova Kasaba 8. The road that we see depicted in the photo, is that the asphalt road leading from Bratunac to Nova Kasaba and Vlasenica, and is this the same road that the 28th Division column had to cut across in order to link up with the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I can answer only the first part of your question and it is yes, it is the road that goes from Vlasenica to -- I mean, Nova Kasaba-Bratunac. I do not know about -- I mean, much about the 28th Division and whether they were crossing or something. I mean, as I told you, I do know in general terms that people were crossing that road, but I mean I'm by no means an expert on the matter. I mean, I know as much as I know based on reading books and having general information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now something that has caused confusion. Now that you have answered Judge Moloto's question, the leaves and branches of the willow tree that were found on the bodies among group 1, are they linked up with Nova Kasaba 5 as a possible execution site? If you can't see it, maybe we should go back to page 4 in B/C/S and in English. This is where you speak about that. Let us look at that. Thank you. Let's look at the last sentence before Konjevic Polje 1. This is where you say the presence of willow leaves and branches in close association to the bodies of cluster 1 could link them to Nova Kasaba 5 as a possible execution site. In your report further on when you elaborate on this issue on page 20, you also mention the possibility that some of these people were actually executed in the Nova Kasaba 8 grave. Would that be correct and would that correspond with -- correspond to the findings?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is on page 20 in English, to help you find your bearings in the report. Paragraph 4 where there is a reference to three deformed cartridges at the bottom of Nova Kasaba 8. And then it says that those persons were actually executed while they were lying in the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this part correspond to your opinion that we find on page 4?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, but we have to distinguish two different things here. We have a factual link between Nova Kasaba 5 and cluster 1 of Nova Kasaba 8. The factual link are the willow trees, so that's issue number 1, meaning that since that tree is the only tree in the area and you got a scraping area, two tracks, a small mound that contains shell casings, the bodies could have been shot there, collected with a machine, pushed the tree, get some branches, and then taken back to the grave to cluster 1. That's issue number 1. Issue number 2 is whether or not, and the answer is yes, we found slugs under some of the bodies of cluster 1 in Nova Kasaba 8. What does it mean or what is my interpretation of it? That people could have been shot in this case, again why not, while in the grave. There is no -- not too many explanations. I am not speculating here whether the people died or didn't die at Nova Kasaba 5. All I have is shell casings, an area of scraping, tracks, and all the rest of it, and then I got bodies, not all of them but some of them had slugs under them in cluster 1. So there are two separate, I mean, facts, and I have not used the word "execution" in -- in this page 20. I said just shot while lying in the grave. That is the -- the question I was asked a moment ago. I mean, you got the body lying and underneath the body you do find the slug, and this indicates that the person was most likely lying while being shot. So two separate, I mean, facts that have to be taken into consideration here, and I'm not implicating yet again by any means that people were killed. I mean, you can shoot somebody, it doesn't need to be that you are killing the person. But if the person was shot in NK-05, this person ended up in NK-08, and I found slugs underneath it, meaning most likely that the person was shot while in the grave. We could speculate why they did that. That is something totally different. That's another -- another story in itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might just ask again, Mr. Baraybar, is the possibility not there that if the people were shot and killed at NK-05 and then taken by front load payer -- front end loader to NK-08, that they could have been scooped together with the slugs and the bullets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible, Your Honour. Unlikely in this case because you've got matching injuries. Whenever I refer to slugs on the bodies, you have matching injuries on the body and the slug below. That is why it was affirmed that people may have been shot while in the grave. There is one instance in one of the Nova Kasaba sites, I cannot recall which but it is in the report, where you can actually see the excavation and you can see the wall or the profile of the excavation and you can see a body that is lying, and you're looking at the head and the arms extended, and you can see the slugs how they went through the body and they match with injuries on the arms, on the torso, and on the head, so it is rather this than scooping elements that were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I again ask you something about the use of the words "bullets" or "slugs"? I see in the portion we looked at that -- let me see -- and I'm looking at page 20, it reads: "Three deformed 7.62-millimetre bullets and one jacket." Now, is my understanding correct that bullets usually deform after the projectile has been shot and hit something rather than that it deforms without having been fired? And would that be an indication that the word "bullet" might well be used here for the projectile itself which has left the cartridge when fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honour. I think that the whole confusion starts with the use bullet. If I had to redo this now, I would use "slugs" and not "bullets," and I would use bullets as unspent cartridges. Elsewhere in the reports, whenever I refer to bullets in that sense, meaning an unfired ammunition, I would have used unspent cartridge as that, but by "bullets" here and "deformed bullets" I mean a deformed slug, something has impacted something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic. And when I was reading on page 20 -- I was reading from P2086.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the summary for Konjevic Polje 1 together, Professor. In B/C/S it's page 5 as well as in English, the first paragraph, as well as the last two lines on page 4 of the same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, it is T2086.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Briefly, Professor, I will try to deal with something that was unclear to me while preparing for your testimony. There, you say that the bodies of nine persons were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the next page in English? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The bodies of nine individuals buried in two clusters were found. Then in the following paragraph, you say a Seiko wrist watch that stopped at 12.35 on Friday, 15, suggests that the person stopped moving (i.e. died) between 32 and 36 hours before. That is on the 13th. And you refer to Mr. Mills's report of 1999. I would like to ask you the following, and I would kindly ask to you bear in mind page 24 of your report where you comment upon the photograph. I am confused by this. You say a Seiko wrist watch stopped at 12.35 on Friday, the 15th. Did you have in mind the 15th of July 1995 as the day indicated by the wrist watch and the day being Friday? Why do I ask this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me cut it short, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to our checks, the Friday was the 14th of July. And then if we went back and calculate the time, as determining when the person died and stopped moving would be different. If we place this in the context of events it poses a completely new background. Professor, where did you get this information?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The information was, I'm quoting here, Mr. Mills who did the examination of the watches. Now, you are right, you are totally right. In some watches, I mean wrist watches, you have this combinations of sometimes Saturday, 15th or Friday, 15th, and that inconsistency has been noticed. The majority of the -- of the watches, though, indicated as far as I remember Saturday, the 15th, but in some occasions we did find Friday the 15th. Obviously, it has been borrowed from Mr. Mills. The issue of the calculation of the -- of the hours. Understanding as well that after examining -- I mean, he examined a number watches, the real day and date combination were Saturday the 15th and not Friday the 15th, so I am pretty much borrowing the testimony of Mr. Mills in this regard. But it is true that some watches, and perhaps that report will refer to the specifics of how many watches, had this Friday 15th. But it is an inconsistency if we are looking at July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us arrive at some kind of conclusion based on all of this. My reasoning is the following: Based on that piece of information obtained from the wrist watch, the moment when the person stopped moving could become quite relative, in terms of whether it was 36 hours starting from Friday and going back or is it 36 hours starting from the 15th of July and back. Could we agree that my reasoning, in terms of uncertainty as to when the person stopped moving, is correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, I would not really give you an opinion because it pertains to watches and I'm not really a specialist in watches. I would refer to Mr. Mills' report in that regard. However, what is very clear is that -- and that's what I learned about it from Mr. Mills -- is that wrist watches operate by the movement of the wrist. Therefore, your wrists have to stop moving. If you look at the picture on page 28 in the English report, you can see the body with the watch on his wrist. So definitely there is a causal relationship between the body or the wrist stop moving and the watch stopping. I mean, the watch was on somebody's wrist. However, I may want to remind you that irrespective of this piece of evidence, in that grave we found ID cards that linked to people last seen at a specific date and those individuals related to Srebrenica, of course in this case, by the book of the missing of the ICRC, so the dating, if you wish, of the grave have not been based solely on the watch with inconsistency you have already pointed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us look together at the English page 23 which I believe is in front of you. In the B/C/S it is page 24. It discusses Konjevic Polje 1 where you say -- Your Honours, the 5th paragraph -- that the turf found under the bodies suggests that some, if not all, of the bodies were scooped (i.e. with a front end loading) from a different location and then put in the grave. Could you at any point in time conclude whether these bodies had spent a certain amount of time on the surface before having been buried in the Konjevic Polje 1 site?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: We did not find any evidence of advanced decomposition yet again as -- as speaking of maggots, the mass, for example, on the bodies are present. I mean, there was nothing obvious regarding that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, just briefly, I'm interested in one sentence. Are you familiar with Professor Lawrence's position who addresses the fact that the presence of traces of insects after a body had spent three years in the ground is completely unreliable and something that cannot be checked whatsoever? I believe you also mentioned that in some of your previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I am not familiar with Professor Lawrence's statement regarding this matter, but I mean let's be very clear about one thing: Anybody left outdoors, even for five minutes, could have fly eggs being positioned in body orifices, nose, mouth, ears, whatever. And depending on the place where this body could be disposed, these eggs will turn into larvae and so on, so it is not true that you need to have bodies lying on the ground for hours, for days in order to be attacked in this case or being seeded by flies. Flies will operate very fast, and if it's outdoors, unless you are in a very cold climate, very extremely cold climate, I mean, they will just put their eggs, and from the eggs come the larvae. So I am not using at any point in time here this as an element of timing or dating, but it would be obvious if we had found, for example, bodies that were full of fly pupae; that is, the transition from larvae to pupae and then to flies again on a body to tell me, well, this body has been colonised and the -- the -- the area where this body has been buried would have allowed these larvae to turn pupae, for example, and that was not the case. So obviously it's not an exact science in that respect, but, I mean, I did not find a body that was in such a state that I would have said, okay, this person has been lying for, I mean, for weeks outside and then buried. We did not find such a thing. Bodies were quite complete and there were larvae, of course, as expected in any -- pretty much in any -- in any body that had been outdoors, but I mean nothing specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, in your question reference was made to some of your previous testimony. Could you assist me in where exactly I would find what you referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not have a reference off the cuff. I will be able to provide it to you. But based on the questions we put to Professor Wright, we discussed the very same topic, and if you recall, we referenced it through the Popovic transcript, although I do not have that precise reference at this point. Perhaps I could find it, but it would be time consuming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But so when you were referring to the witness's previous testimony, would that not then be in the Krstic case? Because we have no other evidence from the witness than the evidence in the Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By circumstance, I happened to listen to Professor's testimony in the Popovic case and this is why I asked. I believe Professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then, of course, the Chamber is unable to follow that line of questioning or unable to verify. Now, I'm asking you because there may well be a -- some confusion. Did you intend to refer to the possibility that even if flies or maggots or pupae would have been there, that you might not find them any more after three years? Is that what you're referring to? And that therefore not finding it after three years doesn't say that much about whether the bodies had been at the surface "yes" or "no." Is that what you were hinting at? If so, then from the answer, it seems to me that the witness has totally misunderstood your question. But again, that's the risk of unclear references, because the witness did not express himself in any way on the question as I just now rephrased it and if that is the question you wanted to put to the witness. And that's unclear to me as well. Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Also, Your Honours, if today's temporary transcript page 73, starting at line 5, the question was put to the witness and it says: "Are you familiar with Professor Lawrence's position who addresses the fact that the presence of traces of insects after a body had spent three years in the ground is completely unreliable and something that cannot be checked whatsoever?" I think this is misrepresenting Dr. Lawrence's evidence and I could -- and if Mr. Stojanovic could give me a transcript reference to that, because the transcript reference that I have is at line -- transcript page 14800 and the question was put to him: "Entomology being the study of insects having..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: It's at -- but this is not what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are talking about our transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And this is Dr. Lawrence's transcript in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And that's -- I'm just saying we should be fair to the witness. When you're putting Dr. Lawrence's evidence, you should be accurate and Dr. Lawrence was asked if the bodies were in the ground for several years, would you expect such entomological evidence to even still be there, and the answer given --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: The answer given was: "I don't know." And that was at line 14 at transcript page 14800, and this is from the 19th of July, 2013, which is a misrepresentation of Dr. Lawrence's evidence. He did not -- unless I'm missing the -- the transcript reference that Mr. Stojanovic is referring to, Dr. Lawrence did not articulate any of the words that were used in Mr. Stojanovic's question at line -- starting at line 5 at today's temporary transcript 73, and that's -- I just wanted to put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe Mr. Stojanovic, as you answer that question you might as well answer what you mean by completely unreliable and something that cannot be checked whatsoever, because I didn't understand this question when you posed it. Unreliable in doing what? Unreliable for what purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your assistance. I will try to clarify it with a few questions and you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The theory of our case, Professor, is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, just first of all Madam Lee has raised an objection to your question, and I just sort of tagged along that question because it relates to the same passage, so maybe you would like to respond to her objection first.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Lawrence did discuss it, as was quoted in the transcript. It was on the 19th of July when my learned friend was examining them. This is how he answered although the answer was broader encompassing the part I wanted to ask the Professor about. For the time being, since I don't have the reference, I will focus only on that part, and I readily acknowledge that I do not have that reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, after a set of remains has spent three years in the ground, are any traces of insects lost, such as ones which would indicate that the body had spent a certain amount of time on the ground before being buried?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I do not know how to answer the question because let me -- let me paraphrase, and if you could tell me whether what I'm asking is right in order to answer the question: I believe that what you're trying to ask me is whether we have evidence that the bodies were lying outdoors for a while and then buried and see whether the findings in the grave or in the examination would prove or disprove the fact that there was a long interval of time in which bodies were lying on the ground before being buried. Is that what you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, although my correction would stand in terms of a longer period of time. I have in mind any period of time because in the context of this case, it is a relative matter.

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, the answer would be no, but let me explain you why. Whenever death occurs, okay, I mean, whenever death occurs you have various waves of insects invading the body and this depends on humidity, depends on weather, depends on vegetation. It would be totally different to have a body left outdoors in Norway during the winter and a body left in a tropical place in the summer, and it would be totally different because it will have various waves of insects. However, it is normally accepted that flies are the first insects to arrive. That's the usual thing. There are different kinds of flies and they arrive at any moment in time in which the body is dead and it is outdoors, okay? So it is not whether it was five minutes or ten minutes or something. It was much more time. Of course, they are going to come in loads and colonise it. But short time is enough for them to leave their eggs, lay their eggs, and the eggs will become maggots. Now, all the remains we have found, as far as I remember, were colonised by maggots, implying primarily that they were at some point colonised by flies that left their eggs. We have not been using, though, the existence of maggots to try to estimate the post-mortem interval as you would do in a body found in a forensic context nowadays because they were buried. And what we do know is that some of these development to maggots took place while buried, so they went from eggs to maggots because the environment in which they were found, I mean these graves, could have all the conditions of humidity, temperature and so on, and food, for these maggots to feed. But we have never attempted to do a post-mortem interval based on those findings. All we can say is that the bodies were dead, outdoors, and therefore colonised by flies. Whether they were colonised in the first five minutes or two hours or two days or something is -- would be a speculation because there is no point in trying to elaborate on that, as Professor Lawrence may have said. I mean, there is no point in dealing with that. But that you have the maggots in -- while the bodies were in the grave, yes, I mean, they were there, they were full of maggots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there seems to be a bit of a -- I see on that same page 14800, he was asked: "Did you see any evidence of things like pupal cases or other entomological evidence in the remains that you looked at that would be of assistance assessing the time of death?" The answer was: "The short answer to that is no. In Cancari Road 12 we did find some small maggots, but I suspect that they are a consequence of reinfestation of the body once they'd been exhumed and that they would not be of any use in assessing the time since death." So there seems to be a difference in factual observation on what was found. I'm looking at the clock and I should have done that already four minutes ago. Mr. Stojanovic, where are you? You said you hoped that you could finish today. Have you finished or how much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but I believe we still need to address Glogova 2 which will require another half an hour tomorrow, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Half an hour you would still need. As matters stand now, Ms. Lee, any need for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Not at the moment, or if there is, it's not going to be long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Baraybar, we cannot finish unfortunately today. You've heard that we might not need much time tomorrow to conclude your testimony. I'd like to instruct you not to speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or whether it's testimony still to be given tomorrow. We would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom, I. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, for the transcript, I wanted to inform you that in the meantime we have D00353. Its translation was uploaded into e-court under 060656. Also, a translation for D00349 has also been uploaded into e-court as 1D060691.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the parties assist me? Was the only reason why D353 and D349 were not admitted yet is because there was no translation or were there any other objections? If could you revisit the matter tomorrow morning first when the witness enters the courtroom, and could you also have a look at the translation as it has been uploaded. We will then decide on D353 and D349 first thing in the morning. We adjourn for the day with apologies to all those who are assisting us for going beyond the time. And we will resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 3rd of September at 9.30 in the morning.
